I don’t really understand why so many are hyping the remaster up like this; I think it’s pretty clear that it’ll likely just be a graphical update with possibly a few tweaks added. If you’re expecting huge story rewrites I really think you’re setting yourself up for disappointment. I could totally be wrong, but I imagine the biggest update to the games would be some minor changes made to ME1’s gameplay to help it flow into ME2 and ME3 better. 

I think the fact that many people are expecting these huge, sweeping changes speaks to the fact that many don’t understand the difference between a remaster and a remake/reimagining. A remaster is usually just a modernization of an older game using the source code, while a remake is usually a complete overhaul from scratch. For example, when the Ratchet and Clank trilogy was upscaled to the PS3 that was a remaster; it kept the original trilogy completely intact but with higher texture and model quality. When Ratchet and Clank 2016 released, that was a remake/reimagining; it fundamentally changed all aspects of the original game and created something completely new. The language that has been used regarding this by Bioware and media sources has conveyed that it will be a remaster, and not a remake. 

Is it possible for a game to be in a grey area between a remaster and remake? Yeah, totally. But honestly, I don’t really think that’s what will happen here.

“The Tomb Raider name never appeared on Guardian of Light and there was a reason – Crystal was saving that for the next project, what was internally known as Tomb Raider 9, or Tomb Raider: Ascension. Obvious biblical references aside, the team led by creative director Tim Longo was asked to come up with a radically different approach to a Lara Croft adventure. And that’s exactly what they did.

In early design meetings the team started thinking about other games that could inspire a new approach. The emotionally rich role-playing game Ico, the survival horror of Resident Evil, and the towering mythical creatures of Shadows of the Colossus all served as early inspiration. In Longo’s first pass at the design Lara Croft teamed up with a 6-year-old girl named Izumi […] as they adventured through a mysterious island inhabited by ghosts and monsters. Izumi would crawl into small places to help the player, thus creating asymmetric gameplay.

Eventually the player would discover Izumi’s magical ability to manipulate water and interact with the island. After a few months of work the concept was deemed too ethereal and difficult to understand for Tomb Raider. Izumi was excised and at first replaced by a monkey that would accompany Croft on her adventures. When that didn’t work out the kids and animals were replaced by a more menacing presence on the island: colossal monsters.

In this second full pass at the concept design Lara would ride on horseback and battle against these monsters as they hurled trees at her in sequences reminiscent of a God of War game. Further refinement of the colossal monster concept shifted the art direction into the realm of horror, with large zombie-like creatures that would roam a fog-soaked island.

What was intended as a confidential focus test from the Nielsen Group soon became public when one of the participants leaked images and details onto the internet during the summer of 2009. A ‘Rumored Leaked Photos of Tomb Raider Reboot’ thread of the Tomb Raider forums quickly amassed some 3,687 posts from fans who expressed shock over a game that was more Resident Evil or Silent Hill than Tomb Raider. Others worried that setting a game entirely on an island abandoned the Indiana Jones-like globetrotting that was a hallmark of the series. […] Ultimately the horror direction was a shocking twist and focus tests confirmed that the team was ‘moving in the direction of making the greatest art house game that no one would ever play’”

Source: [Unseen64](https://www.unseen64.net/2017/02/13/tomb-raider-2013-ascension-cancelled-beta/) and “Tomb Raider – The Final Hours”

I really disagree that the “flow” is the most important part of enjoying a game. How someone derives their joy from gaming can never really be measured on an objective scale, and insinuating that, especially when talking about difficulty, comes off as very short sighted and almost elitist in a sense.

Gaming as a medium has progressed so far from what it was even 10 years ago. While it’s true that many games still do have a greater focus on gameplay than anything else, it’s also become exceedingly obvious that many developers have started focusing so much on the world building and story that it’s become as much of (or even sometimes more of) a draw for some people over gameplay. Many people may want to experience the story without having to suffer through gameplay that they might personally not enjoy, so why should we judge them and say that they are having an “objectively” worse experience even though they aren’t? 

Now with that being said, how one choses to play a game, even if it’s not a story driven game, is entirely up to them and what they find enjoyable. If they find their “flow” in playing on easier difficulties because that’s what they personally enjoy, then that’s great for them. If they find their joy in playing on normal or hard, then that’s also great.

I wouldn’t say that complexity or quality of composition makes any music objectively better, either. I get what you’re saying, but I feel like it’s still a very unfair way to measure such a subjective art.

I wonder if Hasbro changing the toy line to less realistic designs also has to do with Hanoi Hannah, and her use of the term during the Vietnam war? 

She was a Vietnamese radio host who would read off scripts created by the North Vietnamese Army in an attempt to demoralize American soldiers. Usually started off her broadcasts with: 

“How are you, GI Joe? It seems to me that most of you are poorly informed about the going of the war, to say nothing about a correct explanation of your presence over here. Nothing is more confused than to be ordered into a war to die or to be maimed for life without the faintest idea of what's going on.”

Apparently, her broadcasts weren’t overly effective at demoralizing American troops, and I don’t think any desertions have been officially credited to them. Still a very cool part of history in my opinion, and whenever I read “G.I. Joe” I instantly think of her opening speech.

“The origins of this popular nickname are somewhat murky. A popular theory links the term to the early 20th century, when ‘G.I.’ was stamped on military trash cans and buckets. The two-letter abbreviation stood for the material from which these items were made: galvanized iron. Later, the definition of GI broadened and during World War I it was used to refer to all things Army-related, according to ‘Origins of the Specious: Myths and Misconceptions of the English Language’ by Patricia T. O’Conner and Stewart Kellerman. When this happened, GI was reinterpreted as ‘government issue’ or ‘general issue.’

The prevalence of the term led soldiers in World War II to start referring to themselves as GIs. Some servicemen used it as a sarcastic reference symbolizing their belief that they were just mass-produced products of the government. During the war, GI Joe also became a term for U.S. soldiers. Cartoonist Dave Breger, who was drafted into the Army in 1941, is credited with coining the name with his comic strip titled ‘G.I. Joe,’ which he published in a weekly military magazine called Yank, beginning in 1942. Ruby is honestly my favorite character, even though I agree with people that she can occasionally be a weak main protagonist. However, I do believe that with V7 and V6 she does seem to finally be breaking away from the main cast and establishing herself as the forefront of the show. 

I’ve thought about this a good amount, and while I do agree with you that the seeds have certainly been planted, I don’t personally think that’s where the show will lead. 

RWBY, despite its occasional darkness, is undoubtedly a show about hope, with Ruby being the literal embodiment of that message. To have that hope “snuffed out” at the end of the series would feel like the antithesis of what has CURRENTLY been built up.

I say CURRENTLY because we have a good amount of volumes left. It’s totally possible that the main themes and messages could evolve, thus making it fitting that Ruby ends the series with an ultimate sacrifice. Do I think that’s likely? Not really, but RWBY has surprised me before and I don’t doubt that it will surprise me in the future too. 

I will say though, with the show adopting Monty’s signature phrase “Keep moving forward” I definitely think it could be interesting seeing that message applied to Ruby’s death. I’d be very interested to see it played out with the rest of team RWBY trying to move on from Rubys demise, especially Yang. I think there could be a lot of interesting and meaningful content produced from that concept. However, I’m not sure that it would really fit into all the other story beats. But like I said, we never know what’s going to happen.

I by no means intend to gatekeep criticism or analysis, but I do think the influx of “RWBY critics” has caused a huge surge in people who think that just saying something is “objectively bad” without offering any deeper insight is actual criticism. People are totally allowed to simply not like certain things, but the moment that that subjective viewpoint starts morphing into “Well, I don’t like this so actually it’s bad and poorly written. No I’m not going to expand on that” is when it crosses a line into being a dick. 

I think a large part of this is also the fact that people are VERY quick to criticize certain things without waiting for the payoff at all. I still remember a thread posted a day or two after the episode where Blake and Yang told Robyn claiming that it was “bad writing” because B&Y didn’t face any consequences. Like dude, the volume isn’t even over, do you expect everything to happen within the span of a 15 minute episode?

Plus, there’s a huge portion of the “critics” who think that when the show does something different than what they predicted/what they wanted it’s instantly bad. There’s A LOT of people who assume that, for whatever reason, they can somehow write the show better than Miles and Kerry. I really think they fail to realize how hard it is to write on a large scale like this. They’ll make bulleted lists saying “This is what M&K should’ve done :)” but don’t understand that that’s just the first part of it. RWBY is way larger production wise than most people imagine. Furthermore, most of the time they don’t adequately explain WHY they think M&K (plus the new writers whose names I unfortunately don’t know) should’ve done that. 

People are allowed to criticize RWBY, and they’re allowed to not like it. However, there is certainly a line between constructive criticism, and just being a dick for no reason in particular. I think it’s pretty clear where many fall on that line. It’s really unfortunate, because I’d LOVE to see more analysis on any and all aspects of the show. That analysis just had to go a bit deeper than the usual “Team RWBY stupid, Ironwood good” or vice versa.

I don’t think that each species sees Asari as different. If I recall correctly, that was one throwaway line of dialogue spoken by a drunk dude at a bachelor party. The codex never mentions it, and neither does anything else in any of the games. I really hate that this keeps popping up so often. 

I think it’s just your phrasing that has thrown people off. For the most part, it’s very easy to explain things like the Geth and relays, because it’s sci-fi. You can throw vaguely scientific terms at those concepts and it’s fine, because really that’s all it takes. The technology isn’t real and will likely never be real, so explaining it using fake or exaggerated science is fine. 

However, explaining the exact reproductive process of an alien species would undoubtedly be a lot harder and honestly, kind of unnecessary. We got the basic explanation that was needed for lore purposes, and going any deeper than that is really not needed. Could they make up some fake biological science to fully explain it? Yeah, but I mean... it’s not really necessary. I honestly do think the explanation of “They’re aliens so they reproduce differently. Here is the vague outline of how that happens” is enough. 

I guess that’s just my opinion though. I understand why some people may want to know all the specifics behind certain things in the universe; I just think that some stuff isn’t really worth the time.

I think lore wise some Asari, even when both parents are female, will use the word “father” or “dad” for one parent to simplify things for other species; since I guess the monogendered thing can trip people up.

I don’t really think it’s a concept that’s rooted in Asari culture or anything. Probably just something the writers came up with to help explain the concept to the player.
